speaker_role: former admissions officer (guest Chris Tier, certified educational planner and former university admissions officer); host Chris Bell of 'The College Talk Show' is an independent counselor
commercial_incentive: episode carries a mid-show sponsor read for 'Bell College Consulting'; both host and guest are independent counselors who may sell advising services
key_insights: Demonstrated interest is framed as quantifiable 'touches' with a college: opened emails, clicked links, virtual tours, webinars, meeting reps at fairs/school visits, campus visits with check-in, and follow-up with the reading admissions officer
Colleges reportedly use software with an 'affinity scale' tracking these touches, illustrated via a named dean at Connecticut College describing a 20-point scale

Colleges that weight demonstrated interest most heavily tend to be ones with a harder time hitting enrollment/tuition-revenue targets, i.e. they must protect their yield rate rather than being a near-guaranteed first choice
Highly selective/Ivy-Plus-type schools reportedly don't need to track interest closely because they already yield well regardless of an individual applicant's contact history

'Demonstrated understanding,' a term the guest attributes to a named former Rochester/Cornell admissions dean, is distinct from demonstrated interest: it's a qualitative read, via essays and interviews, of self-knowledge plus specific knowledge of what makes that particular college unique
Recommends checking a college's Common Data Set item C7 to see whether it actually reports considering 'level of applicant's interest' in admissions decisions

Argues demonstrating understanding (being able to articulate a school's specific distinctive qualities, e.g. in 'why us' essays) matters broadly across colleges regardless of whether that school tracks interest
specific_numbers_or_facts: Connecticut College reportedly uses a 20-point 'affinity scale' for demonstrated interest, per a named dean quoted by the guest
At Drew University, the guest recalls admitting roughly 6-7 of every 10 applicants but yielding only 1-2 of every 10 admits, from his own admissions-officer experience there

Amherst College is described as admitting fewer than 1 in 10 applicants while yielding 4-5 of every 10 admits, and as reporting on its Common Data Set that it does not consider demonstrated interest, per the guest
notable_or_distinctive: Distinctive for naming a specific dean and a specific college's internal interest-tracking scale, and for attributing the coined term 'demonstrated understanding' to a named admissions dean rather than presenting it as generic advice.
reliability_notes: A mid-episode sponsor read for the host's own consulting business signals commercial framing; specific numeric claims (yield ratios, affinity scale) are recalled anecdotally rather than from cited documents, though tied to named individuals/schools; auto-captions are clean.
